newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian government reserves final say over OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Serbian government reserves final say over OSCE.

text.p: The Serbian government on Thursday made clear it would not be bound by the recommendations of an international mission it has asked to assess the results of disputed local elections.

In response to intense pressure from mass rallies and international criticism, the government invited the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to verify the results of November 17 local elections.
But Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic said the government would need to consider the OSCE recommendations.
"They are here to establish the facts. Naturally whatever the OSCE mission concludes, our competent institutions will have to assess within the organs of the system," he told a news conference.

OSCE sources said its delegation, led by former Spanish premier Felipe Gonzalez, would leave for Belgrade on Friday. "The delegation is likely to return Saturday evening or Sunday," one source told Reuters in Vienna.

Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic invited the OSCE to help defuse a crisis over elections which the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition says it won in 15 of Serbia's biggest towns and cities, including Belgrade, on November 17.
Zajedno says its triumphs were reversed by ruling Socialist party manipulation.
Washington has led Western attacks on what it sees as effective one-party rule in Serbia and has demanded that Milosevic accept defeat in Belgrade and other cities.
It would like to see Milosevic accept the OSCE findings as binding.
Zajedno and student supporters have staged daily protests at the alleged electoral fraud. They drew up to 250,000 people in Belgrade last weekend and have spread to more than 30 towns and cities.
Milutinovic, playing down the crisis, said the demonstrators had the right to express themselves as long as protests were peaceful but said the disputes should have been resolved at home.
"We believe that all this should be resolved within the institutions of the system," he said. "The reaction is totally out of proportion to the issue," he said.
"The opposition has made a point by street demonstrations but it is time to get on with more important matters, like re-building the economy," he added.

Milutinovic said "serious damage has been done" to Serbia's standing in the international community which had improved significantly after Milosevic played a pivotal role in securing the Dayton peace accord for Bosnia.
Washington has warned Belgrade that it would once again become a political pariah and threatened reimposition of sanctions unless Milosevic behaved more democratically.
Milutinovic denied there was a crisis. "The republican and federal governments are functioning without any problems," he said, adding: "Someone out there would like to see Yugoslavia destabilised."
